title: Early detection of severe fetal growth restriction using multimodal deep learning based on ultrasound and prenatal biomarkers

paragraphs.en: Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major pregnancy complication characterized by the failure of the fetus to reach its full growth potential. It is a leading cause of stillbirth, neonatal morbidity, neurodevelopmental disorders, and long-term metabolic and cardiovascular disease.1–3 According to international guidelines, FGR is diagnosed when estimated fetal weight (EFW) or abdominal circumference (AC) is below the 3rd percentile, or below the 10th percentile with abnormal Doppler findings.4–7 In low- and middle-income countries, the prevalence of FGR ranges from 5% to 25%, often overlapping with small-for-gestational-age (SGA) status.1,8

Early identification of pregnancies at risk for FGR is essential for initiating preventive strategies, such as initiating low-dose aspirin before 16 weeks’ gestation in women at increased risk of preeclampsia, which may confer downstream benefits for FGR/SGA, and for guiding antenatal surveillance and delivery planning.9,10 However, current screening methods have limited sensitivity, as subtle placental dysfunctions may not be apparent until late gestation when growth deviation or abnormal Doppler findings occur.5,6,11 Therefore, there is a critical need for more accurate early prediction methods.

Traditional approaches rely on maternal characteristics and serum markers such as pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A) and placental growth factor (PlGF), which offer only modest predictive power.9,12–14 More recently, machine learning models integrating clinical and imaging data have shown promise, particularly those using multimodal frameworks.8,15,16 A model based on first-trimester clinical, Doppler, and biochemical parameters reported an AUC of 0.82, suggesting early detection is feasible.9

Advances in deep learning have enabled automatic extraction of diagnostic features from ultrasound. Some models achieve high accuracy for conditions like Down syndrome using first-trimester imaging.17 However, few studies have explored end-to-end deep learning models for FGR using both first- and second-trimester ultrasound combined with clinical data.

In this study, we present a multimodal deep learning model that integrates standard ultrasound images from early and mid-gestation with maternal serum biomarkers. Our model incorporates attention mechanisms, dynamic convolution, and structured data fusion, and demonstrates high predictive performance in early FGR risk stratification using routine prenatal data.

This prospective study was conducted using data collected from Jinan Maternity and Child Care Hospital Affiliated to Shandong First Medical University, Jinan, China. Ethical approval was granted by the Medical Ethics Committee of Jinan Maternity and Child Care Hospital (Approval No. IIT 0-24-01), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Trial registration: ChiCTR2400085868, http://www.chictr.org.cn. Between July 2024 and February 2025, 13,991 pregnant women were recruited. Inclusion criteria were singleton gestation, informed consent, and compliance with routine prenatal care. Exclusion criteria at enrollment included multiple pregnancy, known fetal structural or chromosomal abnormalities at the time of recruitment, and inability or refusal to provide informed consent. For the present analysis, pregnancies were further excluded due to missing outcome data (n = 982), fetal structural or chromosomal abnormalities (n = 761), or miscarriage before 22 weeks (n = 117). In addition, 1,158 women declined participation. After these exclusions, 10,973 singleton pregnancies remained. Among the eligible cases, 299 pregnancies diagnosed with severe FGR were identified and matched 1:1 by gestational age with 299 controls. Severe FGR was defined as an EFW or AC below the 3rd percentile. The 598 matched pregnancies were randomly divided into training (n = 418), validation (n = 60), and testing (n = 120) sets in a 7:1:2 ratio. These subsets were used to develop and evaluate the prediction model. The study flow is shown in Figure 1.

For each pregnancy, seven standard ultrasonographic images were obtained: (1) crown-rump length (CRL) and nuchal translucency (NT) images at 11–14 weeks of gestation; (2) AC, head circumference (HC), femur length (FL), umbilical artery systolic/diastolic ratio (S/D), and amniotic fluid depth (AFD) images at 19–23 weeks of gestation. After 23 weeks of gestation, fetal growth was monitored by serial ultrasound examinations according to the standard antenatal follow-up schedule, typically every 4 weeks, with additional assessments performed when clinically indicated. Severe FGR was confirmed at or after 24 weeks’ gestation when the EFW or AC fell below the 3rd percentile. All ultrasound images were acquired using the following ultrasound systems: EPIQ7, EPIQ7C (Philips Healthcare, Netherlands), ProVoluson E10 (GE Healthcare, USA), and HERAW10 (Siemens Healthineers, Germany).

Additionally, maternal serum biochemical data were extracted for each participant, including the multiples of the median (MoM) values of PAPP-A and free β-hCG, measured during first-trimester Down’s syndrome screening (11+0 to 13+6 weeks of gestation) using the PerkinElmer (PE) AutoDELFIA method. Maternal age at the time of screening was also recorded for subsequent model development.

The original ultrasound images were stored in the NRRD format, which is not directly compatible with most deep learning frameworks. To facilitate subsequent processing, all NRRD files were first imported into 3D Slicer, where regions of interest (ROIs) were manually delineated by trained experts. After the annotation was completed, the NRRD images were sliced into individual 2D sections. For each slice, the annotation mask was overlaid onto the original grayscale image in a semi-transparent manner to enhance visual clarity. The resulting composite images were then saved in standard two-dimensional PNG format, ensuring compatibility with mainstream computer vision frameworks.

After conversion, each image underwent automated cropping to remove non-clinical content such as text annotations, borders, and scale bars. All images were then resized to 224 × 224 pixels to match the input requirements of the neural network. Gaussian filtering was applied to suppress noise, and histogram equalization was used to enhance contrast and highlight anatomical structures.
To improve the model’s generalization and robustness to fetal morphological variation, we applied data augmentation techniques during training. Specifically, we used:
Random rotation within the range of −15° to +15°, which helped the model learn to recognize anatomical features under varied imaging angles and reduced sensitivity to acquisition orientation;
Horizontal flipping, which leveraged the approximate left–right symmetry of fetal anatomy and prevented the model from overfitting to fixed anatomical orientations.

A standardized data structure was ultimately established: all PNG images were organized into separate folders according to a predefined naming convention, while clinical data and label information were centrally stored in a CSV file. This structure ensured one-to-one correspondence between imaging and phenotypic data during subsequent model training, supporting efficient batch processing and streamlined model loading.

To improve the accuracy and generalization ability of severe FGR risk prediction, we propose a deep learning-based classification model that integrates multi-level attention mechanisms, Dynamic Convolution, and multimodal fusion strategies. The model is designed to identify early imaging features and structured clinical indicators predictive of FGR in the second and third trimesters of pregnancy, leveraging local-global collaborative feature modeling and adaptive convolutional modulation. Additionally, structured clinical information is incorporated to support decision-making. The overall architecture of the proposed model is illustrated in Figure 2.

Multi-level feature extraction backbone: The model employs a stacked Basic Block structure as its backbone, with layer depths configured as [3, 4, 6, 3], enabling hierarchical extraction of features with different semantic levels. At each stage, we integrate Local Attention and Global Attention mechanisms to enhance both fine-grained detail recognition and global contextual understanding.

Local Attention focuses on a limited spatial neighborhood, enabling the model to capture fine structural cues such as edges, textures, and subtle anatomical variations—critical for detecting small-scale abnormalities. In contrast, Global Attention models long-range dependencies across the entire feature map, allowing the network to aggregate holistic contextual information and understand broader spatial relationships, such as organ symmetry or inter-regional patterns.

This dynamic adaptation allows the model to select optimal convolutional responses conditioned on the input structure, thereby improving its robustness to morphological variability and complex feature distributions commonly found in osteoarticular imaging data.

In addition to the above modules, we introduce a prediction-level fusion strategy to exploit the complementary information between clinical structured data and imaging features. Specifically, image data and clinical data are processed through independent sub-networks to generate intermediate prediction vectors vimg and vclin, respectively. The clinical features (e.g. maternal age, gestational week, PAPP-A, β-HCG), extracted from CSV files, are first projected into a low-dimensional embedding space via a fully connected layer.

The fused vector vfusion is then fed into a final classification layer to generate the overall prediction. This architecture allows each modality to contribute independently before synergistic integration, improving model robustness and decision accuracy, especially in cases with missing or ambiguous information in one modality.
To validate the effectiveness of our proposed model, we compared it with several representative deep learning architectures, including both classical CNNs and transformer-based models:

ResNet-18/ResNet-50: Classic residual networks known for effective feature extraction. ResNet-50 provides deeper representation capacity, while ResNet-18 offers lightweight design suitable for real-time or resource-constrained settings.
DenseNet-121: Utilizes dense connections between layers to promote feature reuse and improve gradient flow, particularly effective on small-scale medical image datasets.

MobileNetV2: A lightweight network based on depthwise separable convolutions. It achieves fast inference and low computational cost, although its performance in complex multimodal fusion tasks is relatively limited.
InceptionV3: Employs multi-scale convolution kernels to extract diverse spatial features, making it well-suited for heterogeneous medical images.
Traditional CNN: Serves as a baseline with standard convolutional and pooling layers, offering a reference point to evaluate architectural improvements.

Vision Transformer (ViT): A transformer-based model that uses self-attention for global feature modeling. It is effective in capturing long-range dependencies and has shown promise in complex medical imaging tasks.
All models were trained and evaluated under the same experimental settings. Performance was assessed using consistent metrics.

To comprehensively evaluate model performance, we adopted four widely used classification metrics: F1-score, Precision, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), and Accuracy (Acc). These metrics collectively assess both the predictive power and robustness of the model, especially in the context of imbalanced clinical data.
Precision (Pre) measures the proportion of correctly predicted positive samples among all samples predicted as positive, reflecting the model’s ability to avoid false positives:
F1-score (F1) is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced evaluation metric that considers both false positives and false negatives:
MCC is a correlation-based metric that takes into account all elements of the confusion matrix (TP, TN, FP, FN). It is particularly suitable for evaluating performance on imbalanced datasets:
Acc represents the proportion of correctly classified samples among all samples:

All metrics were computed on the held-out test set to ensure unbiased evaluation. For binary classification tasks (e.g. FGR vs. normal), threshold-based predictions were derived from the model’s output probabilities. For fair comparison, all baseline and proposed models were evaluated under identical experimental conditions.

This study’s design and reporting adhered to the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD), as detailed in Table S1. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 26.0) and Python (version 3.9). Continuous variables were assessed for normality and summarized as medians with interquartile ranges; Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used for group comparisons. Categorical variables were compared using Chi-square tests. Predictors – including seven standardized ultrasound images and maternal variables (age, gestational age, PAPP-A and β-hCG MoM) – were directly included without feature selection. Images were preprocessed and augmented before input into an end-to-end deep learning model with attention and dynamic convolution. Clinical variables were embedded and fused with imaging features at the classification stage. Internal validation was performed using five-fold cross-validation. Model predictions were probability scores converted into binary outcomes. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, F1-score, MCC, and AUC based on ROC curves; confusion matrices were used to evaluate classification performance.

In this section, we present the overall workflow of the model through pseudocode to provide a clear and structured overview of the model’s process. As shown in Table 1, it outlines each key step from data input to final prediction, highlighting the sequential operations performed by the model, including data preprocessing, feature extraction, dynamic convolution, the application of attention mechanisms, and multimodal data fusion.

Based on the final dataset described in the Methods section, a total of 598 singleton pregnancies were included, comprising 299 cases diagnosed with FGR and 299 gestational age–matched controls. Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 2 and Table S2. No significant differences were observed between the Control and FGR groups in maternal age, gestational age at first-trimester ultrasound, or second-trimester ultrasound (all p > 0.05). However, the FGR group had significantly lower birth weight (2400 [2110, 2760] g vs. 3300 [3050, 3600] g, p < 0.001) and earlier gestational age at delivery (37.2 [34.25, 38.5] weeks vs. 39.1 [38.15, 39.36] weeks, p < 0.001). The distribution of neonatal sex did not differ between the groups (p = 0.164).

All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4080 Super GPU with an Intel Core i9-14900KF CPU. The dataset included paired ultrasound images and clinical annotations, which were preprocessed and split into training, validation, and test sets at a 7:1:2 ratio. To ensure robustness, five-fold cross-validation was performed, and average metrics were reported across folds, including comparative and ablation experiments. The model was optimized using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum and cross-entropy loss. A learning rate scheduler was applied to improve convergence and avoid local minima. Model performance was evaluated using Precision, F1-score, Accuracy, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). Interpretability was enhanced using ROC curves for threshold analysis, confusion matrices for classification alignment, and Grad-CAM heatmaps to visualize salient image regions contributing to predictions.

To evaluate the effectiveness of each key component in our proposed model, we conducted a series of ablation experiments. The baseline model includes only the standard backbone, without Dynamic Convolution, attention mechanisms, or multimodal fusion. Based on this configuration, individual modules were incrementally added to isolate and assess their independent contributions to overall performance. The detailed results are presented in Table 3.

Introducing Dynamic Convolution to the baseline model improved the F1-score from 0.8442 to 0.8543 and significantly increased the MCC from 0.7059 to 0.9308, demonstrating its ability to adapt convolutional operations to morphological variations observed in fetal imaging. Adding local attention on top of Dynamic Convolution produced a slight improvement in precision (from 0.8758 to 0.8776), indicating its role in enhancing spatial feature localization, though overall metrics remained relatively stable.

The full model incorporating Dynamic Convolution, local attention, SE modules, and hierarchical feature extraction achieved further performance gains, reaching an F1-score of 0.8736 and an MCC of 0.7476. Finally, integrating multimodal learning – by fusing structured clinical data (e.g. maternal age, PAPP-A, β-HCG) with imaging features – led to the best overall results: an F1-score of 0.912, precision of 0.91, MCC of 0.7982, and accuracy of 0.911. These findings clearly underscore the value of combining clinical and imaging modalities for robust and accurate prediction of FGR risk.

Figure 3 shows the confusion matrices for each model in panels A to E, representing the Baseline, Baseline + Dynamic Conv, Baseline + Dynamic Conv + Local_Att, Our, and Our + Clinical Data models. Panel F compares the ROC curves for all models, further emphasizing the performance improvements.

To further verify the effectiveness of our proposed model in the task of FGR prediction, we conducted performance comparisons with several widely adopted deep learning architectures, including traditional CNNs, ResNet-18/50, InceptionV3, DenseNet-121, and ViT. The detailed quantitative results are presented in Table 4.

Among all baseline models, ResNet-50 achieved the best performance with an F1-score of 0.8567 and an MCC of 0.7157, followed by DenseNet-121 (F1: 0.8465, MCC: 0.7132) and ResNet-18 (F1: 0.8442, MCC: 0.7059). The standard CNN yielded slightly lower performance (F1: 0.8409), though still competitive. In contrast, InceptionV3 and especially ViT performed suboptimally on this task. ViT produced the lowest F1-score (0.7688) and MCC (0.4884), likely due to its strong data dependency and relatively weak inductive bias for small-scale medical datasets.

Our proposed model outperformed all baselines, achieving an F1-score of 0.8736, precision of 0.8964, and MCC of 0.7476. Moreover, when incorporating multimodal learning by fusing structured clinical data (e.g. maternal age and biomarkers) with imaging features, the model achieved the best overall performance: an F1-score of 0.912, MCC of 0.7982, and accuracy of 0.911. These results clearly demonstrate that our method – especially with clinical-imaging integration – offers superior robustness and predictive accuracy in the context of FGR classification.

Figure 4 presents the ROC curve results, demonstrating the classification performance of each comparative model. The highest AUC is achieved by “Our + Clinical Data” (0.9616). The confusion matrices shown in Figure 5 further illustrates the distribution of true and false predictions across different models, with “Our + Clinical Data” exhibiting the most accurate predictions.

The visualization results shown in Figure 5 illustrate the Grad-CAM-based attention maps generated by the proposed model, covering seven common fetal biometric parameters: CRL, NT, AC, HC, FL, S/D, and AFD. For each parameter, representative samples from both the Control and FGR groups are presented. In each sample pair, the left image corresponds to the original ultrasound image, while the right image displays the associated attention heatmap produced by the model.

It can be observed that the proposed model consistently focuses on clinically relevant ultrasound planes – such as the fetal head, abdomen, femur, and blood flow signals – in both groups. Notably, the attention regions in the FGR group tend to be more concentrated and precisely localized, which may reflect subtle pathological structural differences captured by the model. In contrast, the attention maps in the Control group exhibit a broader spatial distribution, suggesting the extraction of more generalized features.

These visualization results provide intuitive and compelling evidence that, in the image classification task, the model not only learns meaningful discriminative features but also demonstrates a high degree of interpretability in its attention behavior, which aligns closely with clinical understanding.

In this study, we developed and evaluated a deep learning-based multimodal model that integrates routine ultrasound images and early maternal biomarkers to predict severe FGR before clinical manifestation. The proposed model achieved strong classification performance, with an AUC of 0.96, an F1-score of 0.912, and an MCC of 0.7982, significantly outperforming conventional CNN, ResNet-50, and other baseline models. We proposed an end-to-end multimodal deep learning framework that incorporates both first-trimester (11–14 weeks) and second-trimester (19–23 weeks) standard ultrasound views, maternal serum biomarkers (PAPP-A and free β-hCG), and baseline clinical features. The architecture consists of multi-level feature extraction, Dynamic Convolution, spatial attention mechanisms, and SE modules, with feature-level fusion of imaging and clinical data. Model performance was assessed using five-fold cross-validation, with ablation and comparative experiments confirming that each component – especially maternal serum markers – contributed significantly to performance gains. Grad-CAM visualizations further confirmed that the model attends to clinically relevant anatomical regions, supporting interpretability and alignment with obstetric practice.

Our results represent a notable improvement over most existing models for predicting FGR, particularly severe FGR, or SGA. Traditional screening approaches based on maternal factors and serum biomarkers typically achieve only moderate accuracy, with reported AUCs often in the range of 0.75–0.859,.18 In contrast, our model reached an AUC of 0.96 by mid-pregnancy, indicating a substantially higher discriminative capacity. Although differences in population characteristics and outcome definitions may influence comparisons, the observed performance gap likely reflects the inclusion of rich imaging data and the advantages of end-to-end deep learning architecture.

Other recent multimodal frameworks combining advanced imaging modalities, such as placental MRI, with ultrasound and clinical data have achieved external validation AUCs around 0.88.16 Our model achieved higher internal performance using only routine prenatal inputs, suggesting that well-leveraged standard sonographic data can approach or surpass models relying on specialized imaging. Earlier machine learning efforts using mid-pregnancy biometric and Doppler data have demonstrated success in late-pregnancy FGR detection, but typically after clinical signs emerge. In contrast, our approach predicts risk weeks in advance, partially enabled by the novel inclusion of first-trimester CRL and NT views, which may encode subtle indicators of early placental development. Although these early images are not independently predictive, they likely contribute valuable contextual information, particularly when combined with second-trimester biometry.

Our findings also reinforce the importance of multimodal data integration. Incorporating maternal serum biomarkers significantly enhanced model performance, especially in cases where ultrasound findings appeared normal. Low levels of first-trimester PAPP-A and abnormal β-hCG are known to reflect impaired placental function, and their predictive value was confirmed in ablation experiments.12 Similarly, Doppler ultrasound features – such as umbilical artery S/D ratios – provided strong discriminatory signals, consistent with clinical understanding of uteroplacental insufficiency.15 Additional angiogenic biomarkers, though not included in our dataset, have shown potential in complementing Doppler indices for identifying late-onset fetal smallness. Collectively, these results support the consensus that combining anatomical, hemodynamic, and biochemical information offers a more comprehensive assessment of fetal growth potential than any single modality alone.

An important strength of this study lies in its reliance on routinely collected prenatal data, making the model clinically applicable without additional burden. The seven ultrasound views represent core components of routine fetal assessment across early and mid-gestation. First-trimester sagittal CRL and NT views are typically used for dating and aneuploidy screening, but may also carry early signals of placental dysfunction.17,19 Enlarged NT or abnormal ductus venosus flow can reflect underlying cardiac or placental pathology, even in chromosomally normal fetuses,20,21 enabling the model to capture such early deviations. Second-trimester biometry (HC, AC, FL) assess fetal size; although most FGR cases do not meet diagnostic thresholds at this stage, deviations in growth trajectory or lagging AC may serve as early warnings. Previous studies have shown that mid-gestation biometry combined with maternal factors offers modest predictive value for SGA.19,22,23 Our model builds on this by identifying nuanced patterns in image data that may precede overt growth restriction. The Doppler S/D ratio view provides functional insight into placental resistance, a known correlate of FGR risk.24,25 High resistance indices in the umbilical or uterine arteries at mid-pregnancy often indicate suboptimal placentation.26,27 Including this view allows the model to account for both fetal size and hemodynamic status. Similarly, the AFD view reflects fetal well-being, as reduced fluid volume may result from impaired placental perfusion.28 Even borderline low fluid at 20–24 weeks may be indicative of chronic insufficiency. Collectively, these views provide complementary structural and functional perspectives on fetal growth and placental health. The fact that none were eliminated during feature selection underscores their combined value in predicting FGR.

Maternal features were also selected based on availability in routine screening. While maternal age alone is a weak predictor, it is linked to placental complications and included for completeness. First-trimester serum markers PAPP-A and β-hCG are routinely measured for aneuploidy risk but also reflect trophoblastic function.29,30 By integrating these serum markers with imaging at the feature level, the model emulates clinical reasoning – distinguishing constitutional smallness from pathological restriction in cases of suspected placental insufficiency.

Ablation experiments demonstrated the contribution of each architectural module. Attention mechanisms improved sensitivity by focusing on clinically relevant image regions. Dynamic Convolution improved precision by adapting to fetal variability. SE blocks enhanced calibration by refining channel-wise responses. Multimodal fusion had the largest performance gain: excluding clinical features led to a significant drop in AUC, highlighting the complementary value of combining maternal and imaging data. Additionally, our hybrid CNN with attention outperformed transformer-based models such as ViTs, which often require larger datasets. Given the structured nature of ultrasound and our moderate sample size, our model balanced accuracy with computational efficiency.

If validated through multi-center studies, the model could assist clinicians in early risk stratification for FGR. Following a mid-pregnancy scan, it could generate an individualized risk score to inform monitoring, referral, and intervention planning. Identifying FGR risk at 20–24 weeks – before overt restriction – creates opportunities for proactive management.2,13,31,32 This aligns with emerging paradigms in perinatal medicine emphasizing prediction, prevention, and personalization.

Despite its promising results, this study has several limitations. The dataset was prospectively collected from a single center and lacks external validation. Although maternal age and first-trimester serum biomarkers were incorporated, broader maternal health variables, such as pre-pregnancy BMI, smoking status, chronic hypertension, diabetes, and obstetric history, were not systematically included. This parsimonious design was intended to improve clinical applicability by relying on readily available screening variables, but it may have limited the model’s ability to capture the full maternal risk profile. In addition, the ultrasound images were static 2D planes, introducing possible selection bias. Severe FGR was defined by EFW or AC below the 3rd percentile, and pregnancies with fetal structural or chromosomal abnormalities were excluded, which may limit generalizability to all etiologic subtypes of severe FGR. Future work should include multicenter prospective studies with external validation, incorporate standardized longitudinal assessments, and evaluate real-world clinical utility.

This study demonstrates that a deep learning model integrating routine prenatal ultrasound images with early pregnancy biochemical markers can substantially improve the early prediction of severe FGR. The model achieved an F1-score of 0.912 and an MCC of 0.7982, outperforming ResNet-50 by +3.91% and +5.06%, respectively. By combining spatial attention mechanisms, Dynamic Convolution, and multimodal fusion, the model captures both anatomical and physiological indicators of impaired placental function. The use of standard prenatal data ensures real-world applicability, highlighting the promise of artificial intelligence to support earlier and more individualized care for at-risk pregnancies.

figures.label: Figure 1.
figures.caption: Flowchart of participant selection and dataset allocation. A total of 13,991 pregnant women were initially enrolled. After excluding 3,018 pregnancies due to declining participation (n = 1,158), missing outcome/follow-up data (n = 982), fetal structural or chromosomal abnormalities (n = 761), or miscarriage before 22 weeks (n = 117), 10,973 singleton pregnancies remained eligible. Among these eligible pregnancies, 299 met the study definition of severe FGR (diagnosed at or after 24 weeks’ gestation; estimated fetal weight (EFW) or abdominal circumference (AC) < 3rd percentile for gestational age). Controls (n = 299) were selected from the remaining non-FGR pregnancies and matched 1:1 by gestational age at ultrasound, defined as the gestational age at the first-trimester and second-trimester examinations. The matched dataset (n = 598) was randomly split into training, validation, and testing sets in a 7:1:2 ratio for model development and evaluation.

figures.label: Figure 2.
figures.caption: Architecture of the multi-modal FGR classification model. This model integrates ultrasound image features and clinical data for predicting FGR. The image input passes through a backbone consisting of basic blocks with dynamic convolutions, local and global attention mechanisms, and a self-attention module. The structured maternal screening variables, including maternal age, PAPP-A MoM, and β-hCG MoM, are reshaped and combined with extracted features. The concatenated features are fed into the final classifier to predict FGR or control status.

figures.label: Figure 3.
figures.caption: Ablation experiment results. Panels A–E show confusion matrices for various models: Baseline (A), Baseline + Dynamic Conv (B), Baseline + Dynamic Conv + Local_Att (C), Our (D), and Our + Clinical Data (E). Panel F presents the ROC curve comparison for these models, with AUC values indicated for each model.

figures.label: Figure 4.
figures.caption: Comparative experiments results. This figure compares the performance of various models, including CNN, ResNet-18, ViT, ResNet-50, DenseNet, InceptionV3, Our, and Our + Clinical Data. Each panel (A–H) displays the confusion matrix for the corresponding model, showing the true and predicted labels for control and FGR cases. Panel I shows the ROC curve comparison for all models, with AUC values indicated for each.

figures.label: Figure 5.
figures.caption: Ultrasound feature visualization in control and severe FGR cases. This figure presents ultrasound images (left) and corresponding heatmaps (right) for various fetal parameters (CRL, NT, AC, HC, FL, S/D, and AFD). Each row compares control (left) and FGR (right) cases, with heatmaps highlighting areas of interest identified by the model.
